title: Sanballat Never Attacks Before You Move
paragraphs:
Sanballat Never Attacks Before You Move
The Hidden Lesson From Nehemiah That Explains Why Critics Always Arrive When God Begins Building Something Through You
There is a painful moment almost every believer experiences but rarely understands.
You finally decide to obey God.
You finally leave the old life behind.
You finally start reading Scripture consistently.
You finally step into the calling God has been whispering into your heart for years.
Maybe the better question is this:
Why did the opposition wait until you started building?
That is exactly where Sanballat enters the story.
Many Christians know Nehemiah for rebuilding Jerusalem's walls.
Fewer remember the names of the men determined to stop him.
Yet one of them has become one of Scripture's greatest lessons about spiritual resistance.
But the spirit behind the criticism.
The opposition that always seems to appear whenever God's people begin moving forward.

Jerusalem—the city where God chose to place His Name—lay in ruins. Its walls were broken down, and its gates had been burned with fire (Nehemiah 1:3). For ancient Israel, walls represented protection, stability, dignity, and covenant identity. Their destruction was more than military defeat; it symbolized deep national shame.
Nehemiah did not respond with anger first.
He confessed not only Israel's sins but identified himself with them.
Only after prayer did he move into action.
When King Artaxerxes granted Nehemiah permission to rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2), everything appeared to be falling perfectly into place.
Until one verse quietly changes the atmosphere.

"But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they were greatly displeased that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel." (Nehemiah 2:10, ESV)
before a single wall had been rebuilt.
Because darkness often recognizes God's work before God's people fully understand what He is doing.

The Hebrew word translated "wall" throughout Nehemiah is חוֹמָה (ḥōmāh). It refers not merely to stone architecture but to a fortified boundary that protects a people and establishes security. Rebuilding the ḥōmāh symbolized the restoration of covenant life under God's care.
Sanballat understood something many believers forget.
God's people would regain their identity.
The enemy has always feared restored people more than broken people.
When Moses rose, Pharaoh opposed him.
When David was anointed, Saul hunted him.
When Elijah confronted idolatry, Jezebel pursued him.
When Jesus began proclaiming the Kingdom, religious leaders plotted against Him.
When the apostles preached Christ crucified and risen, persecution spread.
Opposition often follows obedience—not because obedience failed, but because it matters.
"If the world hates you, know that it has hated Me before it hated you." (John 15:18)

The Greek verb translated "hates" is μισεῖ (misei) from μισέω (miseō), meaning to reject, detest, or oppose with settled hostility. Jesus never promised universal approval. He promised faithful presence.
Nehemiah 4 records him mocking the builders:
Mockery is one of Satan's oldest weapons because ridicule attempts to make obedience look foolish.
One of the enemy's favorite strategies appears in Nehemiah 6.
Sanballat repeatedly invited Nehemiah to meet with him.
"I am doing a great work and cannot come down." (Nehemiah 6:3)
The Hebrew phrase מְלָאכָה גְדוֹלָה (melākhāh gedōlāh) literally means "a great work."
Notice what Nehemiah refused to do.
Sometimes the greatest victory is refusing unnecessary battles.
Not every accusation deserves an answer.
Not every critic deserves your attention.
Not every invitation deserves your time.
"Like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so He opened not His mouth." (Isaiah 53:7)
Sometimes silence is confidence that God is the final Judge.
One of the most overlooked details in Nehemiah is that the builders worked with one hand while holding a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 4:17).
Many believers expect one season for growth...
The moment you build your marriage...
The moment you restore your family...
The moment you commit to purity...
The moment you begin sharing Christ...
But because kingdom work always threatens the kingdom of darkness.
"For a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries." (1 Corinthians 16:9)
Notice that Paul did not say the adversaries proved the door was closed.
The adversaries confirmed the opportunity mattered.
Many people assume criticism means they should stop.
Sometimes criticism is evidence that the wall is actually rising.
Yet Scripture also gives an important caution.
Not every critic is a Sanballat.

The book of Proverbs repeatedly teaches that wise correction is a gift (Proverbs 9:8–9; 12:1). Faithful rebuke from godly brothers and sisters can expose sin, refine character, and lead us toward greater holiness. We must never dismiss biblical correction simply because it is uncomfortable.
How do we tell the difference?
Godly correction seeks repentance and restoration.
The other tries to pull you away from obedience.
The greatest scandal in history was not Sanballat's opposition.
The perfectly holy Son of God was mocked, beaten, falsely accused, condemned, crucified, and displayed publicly in shame.
Isaiah had foretold it centuries earlier:
"He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities." (Isaiah 53:5)

The Greek phrase ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν (hyper hēmōn) means "on our behalf" or "for our sake." Christ stood in the place of guilty sinners. At the cross, He bore the judgment we deserved so that all who repent and trust in Him might receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the gift of eternal life—not by works, but by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9).
The resurrection declared that sin, death, and Satan had been defeated. Because Christ lives, His people can endure opposition with hope, knowing that no criticism can overturn God's saving purpose.
That is the heartbeat of our theme:
Perhaps today your Sanballat is not a person.
A voice telling you that rebuilding is pointless.
But the God who strengthened Nehemiah still strengthens His people. The Lord Jesus Christ is still building His Church (Matthew 16:18), and He is still restoring broken lives through His gospel.

If you have never turned to Christ, today is the day. Repent of your sin. Trust wholly in His finished work on the cross and His victorious resurrection. He does not merely repair lives—He makes all things new.
And if you are already His disciple, keep building.
Do not surrender your calling because someone laughed.
Do not abandon obedience because someone misunderstood you.
The wall God has called you to build is too important.
One faithful stone laid in obedience may outlast a lifetime of criticism.
